Data: [Wine recognition dataset](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/datasets/toy_dataset.html#wine-recognition-dataset), bundled with scikit-learn. Original source: Aeberhard, S. and Forina, M. (1992). *Wine* \[Dataset\]. UCI Machine Learning Repository. <https://doi.org/10.24432/C5PC7J>. Licensed CC BY 4.0.

The dataset has 13 chemical measurements for 178 wines grown in the same region of Italy by three different cultivars. The question: how well does chemistry alone identify the cultivar, and do a couple of measurements do most of the work?

## Setup

```{python}
#| label: setup
#| warning: false
import sys
from pathlib import Path

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.datasets import load_wine
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
```

This confirms the post rendered with the project's own Python environment. The path should end in `.venv`, then `Scripts` or `bin`, then the Python executable.

```{python}
#| label: env-check
print(Path(sys.executable).parts[-3:])
```

## Loading the data

```{python}
#| label: load
wine = load_wine(as_frame=True)
df = wine.frame.copy()
df["cultivar"] = df["target"].map(dict(enumerate(wine.target_names)))

print(df.shape)
df["cultivar"].value_counts().sort_index()
```

## How the cultivars differ

```{python}
#| label: tbl-wine-means
#| tbl-cap: "Mean of four chemical measurements by cultivar."
summary = (
    df.groupby("cultivar")[["alcohol", "flavanoids", "color_intensity", "proline"]]
    .mean()
    .round(2)
)
summary
```

@tbl-wine-means shows clear separation. `class_0` has the highest proline and alcohol, `class_1` has the lowest colour intensity, and `class_2` has far fewer flavanoids than the other two.

```{python}
#| label: fig-wine-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Flavanoids against colour intensity, coloured by cultivar."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
for name, group in df.groupby("cultivar"):
    ax.scatter(group["color_intensity"], group["flavanoids"], label=name, alpha=0.7)
ax.set_xlabel("Colour intensity")
ax.set_ylabel("Flavanoids")
ax.legend(title="Cultivar")
plt.show()
```

@fig-wine-scatter plots two of those measurements against each other. The three cultivars form mostly separate clusters, with some overlap between `class_0` and `class_1`.

## Classifying cultivars

I fit a standardised logistic regression and score it with 5-fold cross-validation, first on all 13 features and then on only the two from @fig-wine-scatter.

```{python}
#| label: model
X_all = df[wine.feature_names]
X_two = df[["color_intensity", "flavanoids"]]
y = df["target"]

model = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
scores_all = cross_val_score(model, X_all, y, cv=5)
scores_two = cross_val_score(model, X_two, y, cv=5)

results = pd.DataFrame({
    "features": ["all 13", "colour intensity + flavanoids"],
    "mean_accuracy": [scores_all.mean(), scores_two.mean()],
    "sd": [scores_all.std(), scores_two.std()],
}).round(3)
results
```

## What I found

With all 13 features the model reaches a mean cross-validated accuracy of `{python} f"{scores_all.mean():.1%}"`. Using only colour intensity and flavanoids it still reaches `{python} f"{scores_two.mean():.1%}"`. Two measurements carry most of the signal, and the remaining eleven mainly resolve the `class_0` and `class_1` overlap visible in the scatter plot.
